title: A hymn in Malar
hook: a plea to the clouds not to wait, and Ravidas naming his family's work out loud

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Malar, the monsoon raga, opening with eating, drinking, laughing, sleeping, and forgetting dying. Your line was rain. Did an interruption make you look up? Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

Rain, dear cloud. Don't wait even a moment. That's a line from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Malar, given in plain English, and it's spoken the way a farmer might speak to a sky that has been holding back. Rain, beloved, and hold up my mind. It's a rain song in the most literal sense. And a few pages further on, in the same raga, a very different voice speaks to the people of his town about his own family and the work they do. Today: two songs in Malar, and what the rain has to do with both.
screen: `RAIN, DEAR CLOUD.` → `DON'T WAIT EVEN A MOMENT.` → `A DIFFERENT VOICE, SAME RAGA.`

segments.voice: First, the rain. In Guru Arjan's hymn, in paraphrase: rain, dear cloud, don't delay. Rain, beloved, hold up my mind, and let joy and longing fill it. The cloud stands for God's grace, and the dry field is the mind waiting for it. And the rain doesn't choose which field to fall on. Now the second voice. Near the end of Malar stand hymns of the Bhagat Ravidas, and in them he does something striking. He speaks to the townspeople and names his caste out loud: a leather worker, known to everyone. In my heart, he says, I hold the praises of the Lord. In another hymn he goes further. In paraphrase: my family still goes around Benares carrying away dead cattle. And yet now the learned Brahmins of the city bow before their son, Ravidas, the servant of servants, because he has taken refuge in your Name. In Kedara, at dusk, Ravidas let the labels fade. Here, in the rain raga, he does the opposite: he says his label out loud, in public, and doesn't apologize for it. He states the work plainly, work others looked down on, and then says what changed: not his birth, not his family's trade, but the Name. The Gurus placed his words in the Granth, to be sung and bowed to beside their own. Now hold the two songs together. The rain falls on every field alike. The Name, in Ravidas's hymn, falls on a leather worker's son exactly as it falls on anyone. A rain song, then, isn't only about weather. It's about grace that doesn't check your family name first. Your line: the rain song.
screen: `RAIN, DEAR CLOUD, DON'T DELAY.` · `RAVIDAS NAMES HIS FAMILY'S WORK.` · `NOW THE LEARNED BOW TO HIM.` · `GRACE FALLS ON EVERY FIELD.` · then, large: `THE RAIN SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Malar shabad, and let the rain fall evenly. If you can, play a shabad sung in Malar, Ravidas's or Guru Arjan's. If not, sit in the quiet. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone whose work is easy to overlook: the person who collects your trash, cleans the building, cares for the sick through the night. Picture rain falling on their roof exactly as it falls on yours. Hold them there, with respect, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can remember the Name Ravidas took refuge in. If you don't, simply hold the person kindly in mind. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Malar. Guru Arjan's plea to the cloud not to delay, and Ravidas naming his family's work out loud and saying the Name, not birth, is what honored him. Today's word.
Your line: the rain song. Today, thank one person whose work usually goes unthanked, by name if you can, and mean it. Day one thousand one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Hymns from the Malar section, the Gurus' and the Bhagats', Ravidas's among them, are sung in kirtan in Raga Malar, and tradition sings them in the rainy season.
